analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate lower prices for its most expensive prescription drugs.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a committee vote: referred to two House committees and their Health Subcommittee in March 2021, it drew 24 Democratic cosponsors but sat with no further action until the Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would repeal the law that forbids Medicare from negotiating drug prices, and instead direct the government to negotiate prices for the costliest drugs used by Medicare beneficiaries. If a drugmaker refused to agree to a reasonable price, the price would automatically drop to the lowest of several benchmarks, including what other wealthy countries pay. It would also require drugmakers to pay Medicare rebates, at Medicaid levels, for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare enrollees. The bill was referred to House committees and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, who pay out of pocket for prescription drugs and whose premiums and cost-sharing are shaped by what Medicare pays for drugs. Taxpayers also benefit, since Medicare is the payer behind roughly a quarter of the nation's prescription drug spending and lower negotiated prices would reduce federal spending on the drug benefit. Low-income enrollees get an additional, explicit benefit: drugmakers would owe Medicare rebates, calculated at Medicaid levels, for drugs dispensed to people who qualify for low-income subsidies.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the 'noninterference' provision of Medicare Part D, which since 2003 has barred the government from negotiating drug prices or running a formulary, and instead requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices with manufacturers beginning in plan year 2023.

Negotiations would prioritize the drugs that cost Medicare the most: the 40 drugs with the highest total Part D spending, the 40 drugs costing at least $10,000 per beneficiary per year, the 20 drugs with the fastest price increases, and single-source drugs whose cost pushes patients past the annual out-of-pocket cap.

If negotiation fails to produce a reasonable price, the price charged to drug plans would automatically be the lowest of three benchmarks: the price paid under the federal veterans' health program, the median price in Canada, the UK, Germany, France, and Japan, or the manufacturer's average price net of rebates.

Drugmakers would have to pay Medicare a rebate for each unit dispensed to low-income 'rebate eligible' enrollees, equal to the amount by which the Medicaid rebate exceeds what Medicare already collects in rebates for that drug; a manufacturer that refuses would see its drugs excluded from Part D coverage the following year.

The bill keeps plans free to bargain for discounts below the negotiated price, and requires every plan to have a process for enrollees to request coverage of a drug not on the formulary or subject to prior authorization or step therapy.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, who would face government-negotiated prices with a hard floor of international and veterans-program benchmarks on their biggest Medicare sellers, plus Medicaid-level rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees. Higher negotiated prices paid to manufacturers under Medicaid's 'best price' and pricing rules are expressly excluded from the bill's calculations, so the cost falls on manufacturer margins rather than being passed back through other public programs.

drawbacks.text: A government-set price floor tied to foreign and veterans-program benchmarks is a hard price control: manufacturers and many economists argue that compressing prices on the most lucrative drugs reduces the revenue that funds development of new medicines, and the bill does not carve out an exception for novel or high-risk research.

Giving the Secretary authority to set or reshape Part D formularies concentrates significant power in one federal agency; the bill mitigates this by requiring at least two drugs in every therapeutic category, preserving all existing patient-protection rules, and mandating an exceptions process for any drug not covered, but the agency's judgments about 'reasonable' prices would rely on criteria it writes itself within 60 days of enactment.

The compliance burden is real: drug plans would face civil money penalties of $10,000 per day for late reporting and up to $100,000 per false item for the rebate data reporting, and manufacturers would face a parallel reporting and audit apparatus.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core tradeoff is straightforward and heavily weighted toward beneficiaries: Medicare already pays for these drugs with public money, and the bill simply removes the legal ban on bargaining, with an automatic fallback price so negotiation cannot stall. The serious cost is the long-run risk to drug development incentives if prices on top-selling drugs are pinned to international benchmarks, a risk the bill accepts without an exemption for new or breakthrough therapies. The design is aggressive but coherent, and the procedural guarantees for patient access are stronger than in many simpler price-cap proposals.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and then to the Health Subcommittee, and no committee ever took it up, so it died without a vote when the Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act on March 23, 2021, with 13 original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the Committee on Energy and Commerce and the Committee on Ways and Means, and days later was referred to the Subcommittee on Health in each committee.

No further action of any kind appears in the bill's record after those referrals: no hearing, no markup, no floor vote. The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, with the bill still parked in subcommittee.

Drug price negotiation was a marquee issue for congressional Democrats in this period, yet this standalone bill, backed by 24 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans, never advanced through either committee that held it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers are better off, because the bill's negotiated prices, international-benchmark fallback, and low-income rebates never took effect, and Medicare beneficiaries did not receive the lower prices it promised. Members of Congress avoided taking a recorded vote on a measure opposed by one of the largest lobbying forces in Washington.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Brand-name drug makers and risk-averse incumbents

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Medicare Drug Price Negotiation Act on March 23, 2021.

for.name: 24 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; all 24 cosponsors were Democrats, and no Republican signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means Committees
against.role: Committees of referral, led by their chairs
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; no markup or vote was ever scheduled in either committee or their Health Subcommittee during the two-year life of the Congress.

against.name: Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America (PhRMA) and the brand-name drug industry
against.what_they_did: Fought government price negotiation in Medicare throughout this period, spending heavily on lobbying and advertising against negotiation proposals in the 117th Congress.

against.name: Speaker Nancy Pelosi
against.what_they_did: Advanced House Democratic leadership's own broader drug pricing vehicle (H.R. 3) rather than moving this standalone negotiation bill, which never left committee under her leadership.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and all 24 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican cosponsored the bill, and with Democrats holding a narrow House majority, the two committees that controlled its fate never acted.

industries.note: The bill strips manufacturers of the legal ban on Medicare price negotiation and imposes a fallback price set to the lowest of veterans'-program or international benchmarks on their biggest-selling Part D drugs, plus Medicaid-level rebates on drugs dispensed to low-income enrollees, with exclusion from Part D coverage for refusers. The industry's gain from the status quo — un-negotiated U.S. prices — is exactly what beneficiaries and taxpayers would have saved.

industries.industry: Medicare Part D insurers and Medicare Advantage plans
industries.note: Plans would pay less for drugs under negotiated prices but would take on new formulary obligations and a reporting regime with civil penalties of up to $10,000 a day for late or false rebate data. Their savings on drug costs run in the same direction as beneficiaries' savings, since plans pass drug costs back through premiums.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and drug supply intermediaries
industries.note: The bill requires disclosure of price concessions and rebates flowing through the supply chain, reducing opacity in intermediaries' negotiations, while leaving their role intact. Plans remain free to use their own negotiating tools for deeper discounts.
